extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history, philosophy, and social science
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological principles for studying history and social progress: how to derive empirical and scientific laws of social order and development, and how to interpret statistical and individual influences in historical explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between social statics and social dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Social statics - derivative laws are ascertained by analysing different states of society and comparing them without regard to their order of succession; social dynamics - the study in which the consideration of successive order is predominant, aiming to observe and explain sequences of social conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statical analysis to understand simultaneous conditions; use dynamical analysis to trace filiation and causal succession. For dynamics, attempt to trace each leading general circumstance of a generation to causes in the immediately preceding generation (the axiomata media of General Sociology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace filiation generation-to-generation for dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: The branch of social science aiming to explain sequences should, where possible, trace every leading general circumstance of each generation to its causes in the immediately preceding generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that in practice the whole often produces the whole (consensus of influences), so direct filiation from elementary human nature is difficult; nevertheless this tracing is the ideal for establishing causal chains in social evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine statical and dynamical views to find laws of correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not limit inquiry to progressive changes in separate elements; combine the statical view (contemporaneous condition) with the dynamical (progressive changes) to empirically obtain the law of correspondence between simultaneous states and simultaneous changes of elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, observe contemporaneous conditions of each element and how their changes correspond to one another; such combined observation yields empirical laws that, if verified a priori, become scientific derivative laws of development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek a pre-eminent agent (central chain) to simplify filiation
rubrics_metrics.description: If one social element is pre-eminent as the prime agent of social movement, its progress can serve as a central chain to which corresponding links of other progressions are appended, yielding a more spontaneous order of filiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether a single element (the author argues the speculative faculties -- state of knowledge/belief) predominates; taking that element as central simplifies reconstruction of causal succession across complex social facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical generalizations are preliminary, not final scientific laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations from history (empirical laws) are evidence toward establishing middle principles, but they are not the middle principles themselves and remain applicable only within bounds of observation until justified a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat historical generalizations as indications; seek to deduce them from principles of human nature to convert them into scientific theorems. Be cautious about extrapolating empirical trends beyond observed limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of long-range and comprehensive data for slow intellectual changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Because progress of knowledge and changes in opinions are very slow and manifest clearly only over long intervals, determining the general order of sequence requires consideration of the whole past time, from earliest records to present phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid basing laws of long-term social progression on short or narrow datasets; include as wide and deep a historical span as possible when inferring laws of intellectual or social development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comte's three stages as a candidate generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Comte's generalization: speculation on any subject passes through three successive stages — (1) supernatural agencies, (2) metaphysical abstractions, (3) ascertaining laws of succession and similitude (scientific).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider this triadic schema as a powerful heuristic for interpreting broad historical changes in modes of thought, while critically evaluating its limits (author accepts its high degree of evidence for historical interpretation but is cautious about some of Comte's predictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statistical regularities to corroborate causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical regularities observed en masse (e.g., constancy in murder rates, proportions of letter-writers forgetting to direct letters) provide felicitous verification a posteriori of the law of causation in human conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ large-scale statistical records to reveal regularities that individual case analysis cannot; use such regularities to support causal explanations of social phenomena, while noting limits of the data (period length, geographic scope, registry quality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish causation from fatalism; human volition remains causal
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of causation claims human actions are joint results of general laws/circumstances and particular characters; this does not imply fatalism or that individual volitions are irrelevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In applying causal laws to history, avoid inferring that individuals lack agency. Treat individual volitions as causes among others and recognize that collective averages arise while individual cases remain contingent and often powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account explicitly for exceptional individuals and governments
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptional persons (great men) and governments can have decisive influence on the celerity of social movement and may be indispensable links in causal chains; their effects are not neutralized by averaging in relevant historical periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodologically, do not eliminate the possibility of unique, non-averaging agents; analyze when and how exceptional individuals alter trajectories and when general causes suffice. Recognize that their influence affects predictability and timing of change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about overgeneralizing from narrow statistical fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical tables compiled from facts within narrow geographical limits and short time spans can mislead — they eliminate local moral causes and obscure variations across ages or countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare across ages, countries, and regions before concluding about the relative importance of moral, intellectual, or economic causes; acknowledge that different scales of observation yield different inferences about causal power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual condition as a predominant but not sole determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: The intellectual element of a people (beliefs, knowledge, intelligence) is the predominant circumstance in determining progress, but moral and economic conditions are powerful and often consequences limited by the intellectual condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing causes to social progress, prioritize intellectual changes as enabling other improvements, but analyze moral and economic causes too — they interact and may vary independently in different contexts; avoid simplistic hierarchies without empirical support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on precision of prediction due to contingent combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Because historical outcomes can depend on accidental combinations of exceptional individuals and circumstances, much of the law of human affairs (especially celerity and timing) remains inaccessible and predictions are necessarily precarious within human time scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that science can trace general preparatory causes and probabilities, but cannot reliably fix the epoch of specific innovations or the advent of great men; use probabilistic and conditional reasoning rather than deterministic forecasts.
